idiom_name: class Orders private constructor(items: List<Order>) : List<Order> by items
implementation_notes: Interface delegation removes the boilerplate: `List<Order> by items` makes the compiler generate the whole read-only list contract, so the class adds only the domain operations, and the type system keeps List and MutableList apart - a caller holding List<Order> cannot call add. Make the primary constructor private or internal so no caller can inject an unvalidated list, and let the invariants run in init blocks or in factory functions. Read-only is not immutable on the JVM: kotlin.collections.List erases to java.util.List, so Java callers and unchecked casts can still mutate a mutable delegate - delegate to an immutable snapshot (listOf/toList) when the collection must not change under anyone.
pitfalls: List is read-only, not immutable: on the JVM it is java.util.List, so an unchecked cast to MutableList, or plain Java code, can mutate a mutable delegate; snapshot with toList()/listOf().
A public constructor taking List<Order> lets callers construct an invalid collection; keep it private/internal and build through validating factories.
Delegation does not re-validate derived results: map/filter/sorted on the class return plain List values unless the class provides its own mapping functions that re-wrap.
Delegation forwards the delegatee's identity: equals/hashCode follow the interface contract rather than the domain type unless you override them.
